title: Who but You
hook: who but You would do this, Lord, raising the lowly to honor (Maru, Ravidas, ang 1106)
tomorrow: His family carried the dead cattle

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandalwood and castor: the plain plant growing beside the fragrant tree, made fragrant just by standing close. Who did you stand near, and did any of it rub off? Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

Over a king's head, in the old courts of India, an attendant held a canopy. It said, without a word: this one is honored. Now hold that canopy over someone else. Not a prince. A leather-worker from Benares, the man whose trade made people step aside in the street. That is the picture Ravidas paints in one of his hymns, and he can hardly believe it himself. His question, sung in Raag Maru, is today's word.
screen: `A CANOPY FOR THE KING.` → `HELD OVER A LEATHER-WORKER.` → `WHO BUT YOU?`

segments.voice: The hymn sits on Ang 1106 of the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase, it opens: O Beloved, who but You could do such a thing? Then the Gurmukhi gives a name for God that's worth learning: gareeb nivaaj, the one who cherishes the poor. My Lord, Ravidas sings, places the canopy over my forehead. The royal sign, on him. He doesn't soften what he was in other people's eyes. He says, in paraphrase, that his touch was counted as polluting the world, and on that very person the Lord has poured mercy. Then the line at the hymn's heart: You raise the lowly to the heights, my Gobind, and You fear no one. That last part is quiet but sharp. Lifting a person whom a whole town has agreed to keep low takes nerve. Ravidas's Lord doesn't flinch. And then the hymn opens a door. Ravidas names others who were carried across in the same way: Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain. This week we've walked with Namdev, the cloth-printer whose milk was drunk and whose temple turned. Kabir we met earlier in this block. Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain are still ahead on this path. Ravidas lines them up like witnesses: it wasn't only me. The hymn closes, in paraphrase: says Ravidas, listen, holy people, the Lord does everything. So the word is a question that isn't really a question. Who but You. It's what someone says when they've been lifted and know they didn't lift themselves.
screen: `GAREEB NIVAAJ: WHO CHERISHES THE POOR.` · `THE CANOPY ON A LEATHER-WORKER'S HEAD.` · `THE LOWLY RAISED, AND NO FEAR.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T ONLY ME.`

segments.voice: The practice is to lift one person up. Use the sit to choose who. Let faces come: someone overlooked at work, a relative people talk past, a neighbor nobody greets, a kid who sits at the edge. Stay with one. Then decide one small canopy you could hold over them today: say their name in front of others, ask their opinion first, thank them where it can be heard. Nothing grand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Who but You. Ravidas's question in Raag Maru: who but the cherisher of the poor would hold a king's canopy over a leather-worker's head.

Your line: who but you. This week ran from everything is Gobind to Namdev's sultan to Ravidas's city without sorrow. End it by lifting one person today, and leave the credit where Ravidas left it. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, with the same respect given to the Gurus' own hymns, and this one is often sung as a song of thanks for being raised up.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the cherisher of the poor, Ravidas's name for the Lord in this hymn (Ang 1106).

trapdoor: what you thought: a praise line: nobody's as great as You.
what it means: a lifted man's astonishment: who else would hold a king's canopy over a leather-worker?
what a scholar hears: the canopy is royal court language, and the hymn's list of saints turns one man's thanks into a pattern.
